1	# Framework: coding agents for DevSecOps at Papaya
2	
3	> Status: draft v3, for owner review · Updated: 2026-11-09
4	> Audience: a panel of Engineering and Compliance. Each layer ends with what it costs engineers and
5	> what it gives Compliance.
6	
7	## How to read this
8	
9	Eight layers. Each has a **Principle** (tool-independent), **On Papaya's stack** (Pulumi,
10	Serverless Framework, GitHub Actions, AWS, GCP, k0s, Claude Code) and **Audit evidence** (records an
11	auditor can test without asking anyone). Copy-paste detail belongs in `examples/`.
12	
13	| Marker | Meaning |
14	|---|---|
15	| 📖 R*x.y* | Documented. R*x.y* is a ✅/📖 row in `work/02-research.md` that quotes and links the official page. |
16	| ⚠️ R*x.y* | Inference, open question or "What this means for Papaya" conclusion in the research (sections 1.8, 2.9, 3.6, 3.7, 4.6, 5.6, 5.7, 6.5). Reasoned, not documented. |
17	| ⚠️ | Not verified at all, e.g. an illustrative command. |
18	| [design] | My proposal, built from documented parts, untested. Treat as ⚠️. |
19	
20	Nothing here was checked locally (✅): this is a design without access to Papaya's systems.
21	**GĐ-n** = owner-confirmed assumption in `work/01-problem-framing.md` §4; **S-n** = success criteria
22	(§5); **P/A-n** = problems (§1); **D1–D3** = owner decisions in research 6.6; **Options §n** =
23	`work/03-options.md`; **G-n** = gaps; **Q-n** = owner questions (both at the end).
24	
25	---
26	
27	## 1. The decision in one page
28	
29	Engineering and Compliance disagree only about **writes to production**; reads of metadata and all
30	of non-prod are outside Compliance's sentence (framing §3.1). Real customer data is layer 6.
31	
32	**Chosen approach "A + D2'"** (Options §9, owner decision 2026-11-09):
33	
34	1. **Default path:** every prod change is a pull request, approved by a named human who is not the
35	   author, applied by CI. Incidents included ("IaC first").
36	2. **Fallback (break-glass):** only when the PR path cannot be used, a human gets a 1-hour approved
37	   grant and runs an approved command list in a terminal without an agent (layer 7) [design].
38	3. **Nothing standing:** no human or agent holds standing prod write; no long-lived credentials.
39	
40	| Engineering gets | Compliance gets |
41	|---|---|
42	| A free loop in non-prod: read, change, deploy without approval (non-prod is synthetic, GĐ-14). | Every prod change approved **before** apply by a named human ≠ author (GĐ-8, GĐ-11), enforced in GitHub and AWS IAM, outside the agent. |
43	| Read-only prod metadata for the agent. | No standing prod write (S1), no long-lived CI keys (S2). |
44	| Self-service PRs, one approval, same-day ship (S4). | One evidence chain per change; approval and change records ≥ 6 years (📖 R5.2.9; applied to change records ⚠️ R5.7 #2). |
45	| Incident lane: approval wait ≤ 15 min, 24/7 (S7). Decision-to-apply target ≤ 30 min (Options §9); current estimate 11–46 min ⚠️, measured first in rollout. | Agent-side controls as a second layer, not the control of record. |
46	
47	**Where the design falls short, stated openly:**
48	
49	- **The fallback meets the approval rule only partly** (approves a command list, not an applied
50	  change); accepted by the owner (Options §9 Q2). It is a second, process-controlled path, while the
51	  framing asked for one technically enforced path (framing §3.3, Options §7). It stays narrow only
52	  if most incidents are expressible in IaC (unknown, Options §8); layer 7 measures this.
53	- **On GitHub Team nobody sees the prod diff before apply** (⚠️ R4.6 #1; Team assumed, GĐ-5).
54	  Risky prod diffs stop the deploy for a second approval [design].
55	- **Admins can edit the gate**; logged, not prevented (📖 R3.2.2, ⚠️ R3.6 #1). An admin's agent has
56	  the same power, because the agent uses its engineer's GitHub login.
57	- **Some rules are process, not technology:** see "Process rules" in layer 1.
58	- **HIPAA applicability is a legal question** (⚠️ R1.11.1.11); the design treats Papaya as a
59	  business associate, as the brief implies.
60	
61	**Cross-cutting rules** (owner's balance principle, research 6.8):
62	
63	1. **The boundary is IAM and the CI gate.** Server-managed settings are "a client-side control, not
64	   a security boundary" (📖 R1.1.7); local admins can edit endpoint files (📖 R1.1.8).
65	2. **Assume prompt injection succeeds:** OWASP and NIST state there is no full prevention (📖 R6.1.1, R6.1.2).
66	3. **Friction where damage is large, none where it is small**, measured, with a time-boxed escape.
67	4. **Evidence by construction:** the path produces the records.
68	
69	### Roles
70	
71	| Role | Rule |
72	|---|---|
73	| Author (engineer + their agent) | Never approves own change; GitHub blocks PR authors from approving (📖 R3.3.1). |
74	| Approver | Named human in CODEOWNERS; ≠ author, ≠ last pusher (📖 R3.2.3); for an app-opened PR, ≠ the person who triggered it (⚠️ R3.3.4, layer 5). |
75	| On-call approver | Primary + backup, 24/7, on the on-call schedule; wait ≤ 15 min (S7). |
76	| Platform approver [design] | Platform-team member, also on call; one of the two approvers for L3. |
77	| Data owner [design] | Named per tenant; co-approves real-data reads (layer 6). |
78	| Control owner | DevSecOps (1–2 people, GĐ-1); owns policies and metrics; not the only approver. |
79	
80	---
81	
82	## Layer 1 — Identity and access
83	
84	**Principle.** Every action traces to one named human. Nobody holds standing prod write: prod is
85	written by the pipeline role, or in the fallback by an approved, time-boxed grant. Prod reads default
86	to metadata. No long-lived credentials. Prod and non-prod are separate boundaries.
87	
88	**On Papaya's stack**
89	
90	- **The engineer's access is the agent's access.** The agent uses the engineer's AWS SSO cache, and
91	  one portal session reaches every role assigned to that engineer (📖 R2.2.1, R2.2.2). A separate
92	  "agent" permission set does not separate them (⚠️ R2.9 #1). The control is what the **engineer**
93	  holds.
94	- **Process rules** that follow from this (owner accepted them as process controls, D2, D3):
95	  - the JIT terminal and the real-data terminal run no agent, though the grant is reachable from the
96	    same laptop;
97	  - the incident-analysis session is meant to use only read-only roles;
98	  - an agent does not approve PRs. GitHub blocks self-approval only. The auto-mode default block list
99	    names "approving Claude's own pull request", not approving someone else's (📖 R6.3.3), and it
100	    applies only in auto mode. No detection was found (⚠️; `actor_is_agent` in the audit log has no
101	    documented meaning, R3.5.6).
102	- **IAM Identity Center permission sets** (📖 R2.1.1) [design names]:
103	  - `ProdReadMetadata`: metrics, redacted log groups, configuration; no data-plane read on claim
104	    stores; 1 h session, the minimum (📖 R2.1.4). Lambda configuration can hold secrets resolved by
105	    Serverless in plain text (⚠️ R4.4.7), so configuration reads are allowed per service only after
106	    its secrets move to runtime resolution (⚠️ R4.6 #7). Cost: until then the agent reads
107	    timeout/memory from the IaC code;
108	  - `NonProdDeveloper`: broad, non-prod accounts only;
109	  - `InfraOperator-<service>`: assigned only by the JIT flow (layer 7), via a partner product, the
110	    TEAM sample or a small flow on `CreateAccountAssignment` / `DeleteAccountAssignment`
111	    (📖 R2.4.1, R2.4.1b, R2.4.2);
112	  - no standing prod-write permission set.
113	- **SCPs on the prod OU** [design] (SCPs cap member-account principals, 📖 R2.3.1, R2.3.2):
114	  - deny data-plane reads on claim stores except application roles and the approved data-read role,
115	    by `aws:PrincipalArn` (📖 R2.3.8; pattern ⚠️ R2.9 #4). Actions, e.g. `s3:GetObject`,
116	    `sqs:ReceiveMessage`, `states:GetExecutionHistory`, are incomplete and unchecked (⚠️ G13);
117	  - deny `lambda:UpdateFunctionCode` / `lambda:UpdateFunctionConfiguration` (⚠️ R4.6 #3) except
118	    CloudFormation `deploymentRole`s, the Pulumi prod deploy role (if Pulumi manages Lambdas) and the
119	    JIT roles. This closes `serverless deploy function`, which changes config outside CloudFormation
120	    (📖 R4.4.4), and needs `deploymentRole` set on every Serverless stack (📖 R4.4.5);
121	  - a pre-deployed revocation Deny on `identitystore:userId` (📖 R2.4.4); protect the org trail (📖 R2.6.2).
122	  - Limits: 10 SCPs per target, 10,240 characters; no SCP applies to the management account
123	    (📖 R2.3.2, R2.3.4), so whatever deploys SCPs there is the most sensitive role (L3 path).
124	- **Sessions/MFA:** portal session length set on purpose; an IdP session can extend it silently
125	  (📖 R2.1.5, R2.1.6). MFA lives in the external IdP if one is used (📖 R2.1.7).
126	- **CI → AWS:** GitHub OIDC, no stored keys (📖 R3.4.1). The prod role trusts only the `production`
127	  environment of the monorepo, in its `sub` format (📖 R3.4.3, R3.4.4; immutable format assumed,
128	  ⚠️ R3.7 A2), ideally customised with the deploy workflow's `job_workflow_ref` (📖 R3.4.5; on Team ⚠️ G10).
129	- **CI → GCP:** Workload Identity Federation restricted to Papaya's GitHub organization, which Google
130	  requires (📖 R3.4.5b).
131	- **k0s, GCP and Firebase for humans:** same principles; mechanisms not researched (G1–G3). Today
132	  k0s is reached with kubeconfigs, no SSO (GĐ-4, unconfirmed). Interim: no admin kubeconfig and no GCP
133	  owner role on laptops; prod deploys only from CI. Firebase is not on the GCP BAA list (📖 R5.5.3), so
134	  Firebase Hosting must hold no PHI (⚠️ R5.7 #7).
135	
136	**Audit evidence.** Identity Center assignment export (S1); CloudTrail `CreateAccountAssignment` /
137	`DeleteAccountAssignment` per grant (📖 R2.4.2), linked to its approval by request ID [design]; SCPs
138	and trust policies as Pulumi code; IAM Access Analyzer `check-no-new-access` on policy PRs
139	(📖 R2.8.1); quarterly access review of permission sets and GitHub admins.
140	
141	**Cost / value.** Engineers lose standing prod write, keep fast prod reads and a free non-prod loop.
142	Compliance gets least privilege that is enforced.
143	
144	---
145	
146	## Layer 2 — Agent runtime controls
147	
148	**Principle.** Agent-side controls are hygiene, not the boundary. They are central, versioned in git
149	and the same for everyone. Defaults are safe; overrides are measured. The session that reads
150	untrusted content holds as little power as possible (📖 R6.1.2).
151	
152	**On Papaya's stack**
153	
154	- **Delivery:** server-managed settings (available on Team, 📖 R1.1.5) for all laptops. With MDM, also
155	  an endpoint file; by default one managed source supplies most keys, so the two must carry the same
156	  keys or use `managedSourcesBehavior: "merge"` (📖 R1.1.3, R1.1.4). MDM is unknown; both are prepared.
157	- **Baseline** (template: Anthropic's `settings-hipaa.json`, 📖 R5.5.4). All keys 📖 at the row cited:
158	
159	  | Key | Value and reason |
160	  |---|---|
161	  | `permissions.defaultMode` | `default` (Manual). A default, not a lock: users can switch to auto; VS Code remembers the last pick (D1, R6.9.3). |
162	  | `permissions.allow` | Read-only commands Papaya uses, to cut prompts (R6.9.3). |
163	  | `allowManagedPermissionRulesOnly` | `true`, one rule set (D1, owner Q4; R1.2.5). Cost: project and user rules are ignored, so the managed set must carry every deny/ask rule projects need; prompts likely rise (⚠️ research 6.9.4 Q4). |
164	  | `permissions.disableBypassPermissionsMode` | `"disable"`: removes "prompts off" (P3a; R1.2.2). Auto mode stays available (D1). |
165	  | `permissions.deny` / `ask` | Deny credential paths (R5.5.4; `Read(...)` syntax ⚠️ R1.8 #5). Ask for `WebFetch`, which the sandbox domain list does not limit (R1.6.2); cost: a prompt per fetch. |
166	  | `requiredMinimumVersion` | ≥ 2.1.295 (`onFailure: "block"`, R1.5.2) and ≥ the latest fixed advisory at rollout (R6.3.9). It does not end running sessions and fails open on a bad value (R1.1.13). |
167	  | `allowedProviders` + `forceLoginOrgUUID` | `["anthropic"]` + Papaya's org; closes most bypasses on **endpoint-managed** machines (R1.1.15). |
168	  | `allowManagedHooksOnly` | `true` (R1.5.4). |
169	  | sandbox | `sandbox.enabled`, `failIfUnavailable`, `allowUnsandboxedCommands: false`, narrow `network.allowedDomains` locked by `network.allowManagedDomainsOnly` (R1.6.4); `credentials` / `filesystem.denyRead` on `~/.aws` (R1.6.3). |
170	  | MCP, plugins | Layer 4. |
171	  | OTel | Exporter on, content flags `0` (R1.1.20, R5.5.4). |
172	
173	- **Trade-off on AWS credentials.** With `~/.aws` hidden from the sandbox, `aws`, `pulumi` and
174	  `serverless` must be `sandbox.excludedCommands`, which run "with full access", network included
175	  (📖 R1.6.4). So these tools are an egress channel outside the allowlist. Accepted because the
176	  engineer holds no prod write and no PHI read; the deny still stops other programs from taking the
177	  credentials. Stronger option, phase 3: a separate OS user or container for prod-reading sessions
178	  (⚠️ R6.5 #2).
179	- **Session types:**
180	
181	  | Session | Identity | Flags | Enforcement |
182	  |---|---|---|---|
183	  | Daily development (laptop) | non-prod roles + `ProdReadMetadata` | baseline | Auto mode by choice (D1); `--restricted` recommended (D3). |
184	  | Incident analysis (laptop) | meant to be `ProdReadMetadata` only | `--restricted --tools "Bash,Read,Grep,Glob"`, started in an empty scratch directory, not the repo [design] | Process rule (D3, owner Q1–Q2). No Edit/Write/WebFetch (📖 R6.9.1b), but Bash can still write in its working directory (📖 R1.6.3) and call any role in the cache. |
185	  | CI agent (hosted runner) | own GitHub App token; never `production` | `--restricted`, explicit `--tools`; all rules in a managed-settings file on the runner | Workflow file under CODEOWNERS (D3, owner Q5). The file is advisory if `Bash` is in `--tools` (layer 5). |
186	  | JIT terminal | JIT grant | no agent | Process rule (D2). |
187	  | Auto-mode environment (phase 3) | non-prod only | auto encouraged | D1 option (c). |
188	
189	- **Hard limits:** Bash rules are not a boundary (📖 R1.2.6); hooks fail open unless
190	  `"onFailure": "block"` (📖 R1.5.2); `--restricted` cannot be forced on laptops (📖 R6.9.1, R6.9.1c);
191	  on laptops **without MDM**, a different login, an API key or a `CLAUDE_CODE_USE_*` variable skips
192	  server-managed settings, `allowedProviders` included (📖 R1.1.7; ⚠️ R1.8 #3, G11). So S5's
193	  "nobody can turn off all prompts unnoticed" is likely unreachable without MDM (⚠️).
194	- **Auto memory:** engineers review it and delete it after a suspicious session; residual risk with a
195	  named owner (D3).
196	- **Fallback:** switch to `disableAutoMode` if the planted-injection test steers auto mode, a serious
197	  advisory appears, or an audit finds auto mode touched a protected scope (D1).
198	
199	**Audit evidence.** Managed settings in git with PR approvals; `/status` and `claude doctor` from
200	sampled machines (📖 R1.1.18); OTel `claude_code.tool_decision` (`permission_mode`) and
201	`claude_code.tool.blocked_on_user` (`duration_ms`, rubber-stamping signal) (fields 📖 research 6.6
202	D1 metrics; thresholds ⚠️). Settings-change audit events on Team: unknown (⚠️ R1.1.12).
203	
204	**Cost / value.** More prompts than auto mode, partly offset by the read-only allowlist. Compliance
205	gets one organization policy with evidence instead of personal choices (P3c).
206	
207	---
208	
209	## Layer 3 — Change workflow by risk level
210	
211	**Principle.** The level is set by the damage a change can do. One default path above non-prod: a
212	reviewed PR applied by the pipeline, with the JIT fallback (layer 7) as the only other write path.
213	The approver reviews the code change that will be applied. Higher risk adds a second, specialised
214	approver. Incidents use the same path with faster people, not fewer security checks.
215	
216	| Level | What | Examples | Approval | Path |
217	|---|---|---|---|---|
218	| **L0** | Read: non-prod anything; prod metadata | metrics, redacted logs | none | read-only identity |
219	| **L1** | Change in non-prod | deploy a branch to dev; `pulumi preview` on non-prod (it writes state, 📖 R4.3.3) | author only | non-prod roles or PR pipeline |
220	| **L2** | Routine prod change in code | Lambda timeout/memory, ECS desired count, release, `CLAUDE.md` | 1 code owner ≠ author, ≠ last pusher | PR → `main` → deploy workflow |
221	| **L3** | High-risk prod change | IAM/SCP; replace/delete of stateful resources; network; `.github/**`, CODEOWNERS, `.claude/**`, `.mcp.json`, plugin/MCP catalogue; policy violation | 2 distinct humans, at least one platform approver | same path, second approval by path rule or risk stop |
222	| **L3-JIT** | Break-glass | ECS force-redeploy while Actions is down | on-call approver ≠ requester (Options §4b) | layer 7 |
223	| **L3-data** | Real customer data read | one tenant's failed claim record | data owner + approver ≠ requester, with an agreement (GĐ-9) | layer 6 |
224	
225	`CLAUDE.md` is L2, not L3, so that moving shared knowledge into it (D3) stays cheap.
226	
227	**On Papaya's stack**
228	
229	- **Gate = merge to `main`.** On Team, environment reviewers do not exist for private repos
230	  (📖 R3.1.2). Ruleset on `main`: PR required, 1 approval, code-owner review, dismiss stale approvals,
231	  approval by someone other than the last pusher, required checks from a pinned source app, no force
232	  push, empty bypass list (📖 R3.2.2, R3.2.3, R3.2.5). Branch up to date before merge, since there is
233	  no merge queue (⚠️ R4.6 #1; whether updating drops approvals is open, Options §8).
234	- **L3 approvals [design]:** a path rule requires 1 platform approval on L3 paths (📖 R3.2.4). Because
235	  any one code owner satisfies code-owner review (📖 R3.2.7), one platform member could satisfy both
236	  rules alone (⚠️ inference); a required check with a pinned source app (📖 R3.2.5) therefore confirms
237	  two distinct human approvers. At 2 a.m. this needs the platform on-call plus one other approver.
238	- **Risk stop [design]:** the deploy job previews prod; on stateful replace/delete, an IAM change or a
239	  policy violation it stops. A second PR adds `deploy-approvals/<sha>.yaml` with the preview hash; a
240	  platform approver other than the first approver approves (checked as above); the job continues only
241	  if the hash matches (Options §1; hash stability ⚠️ Options §8). Preview output is filtered for
242	  outputs and secrets before it is posted (Options §1; ⚠️ R4.6 #2).
243	- **Merge approval = deploy approval** only if (⚠️ R3.6 #1, from 📖 R3.1.3, R3.4.5c): `production`
244	  allows only `main`; only the reusable deploy workflow (under CODEOWNERS) references it; no ref/SHA
245	  inputs; no `issue_comment`, `pull_request_target` or `workflow_run` triggers; one concurrency group
246	  per stack without `cancel-in-progress` (📖 R4.1.4).
247	- **Pulumi:** PRs preview non-prod only, because a prod preview runs PR code with state-write and
248	  secret access (📖 R4.3.3, R4.3.4; ⚠️ R4.6 #2). On `main`: prod preview, then `pulumi up` with the
249	  policy pack, which stops on a mandatory violation (📖 R4.2.2). Prod runs allow no `--skip-preview`
250	  (📖 R4.1.2) and no targeting, replace, `state`, `import`, `destroy` (⚠️ R4.6 #3, G12). Pulumi Cloud,
251	  if used: OIDC via `pulumi/auth-actions`, no stored token (📖 R4.1.4).
252	- **Serverless v4:** `serverless package`; `serverless diff --json` (sf-core ≥ 4.37.0), parsed by CI
253	  because differences do not change the exit code (📖 R4.4.2); `serverless deploy --package`
254	  (📖 R4.4.3); a least-privilege `deploymentRole`, which cannot be removed later and is usable by
255	  anyone who may operate the stack (📖 R4.4.5), so JIT roles get no stack-operation rights.
256	- **State:** writable only by deploy roles; readable also by the drift role (layer 7); Pulumi
257	  secrets via `awskms` on a DIY backend (📖 R4.3.3, R4.3.4; ⚠️ R4.6 #7).
258	- **k0s [design]:** manifests in the monorepo, applied by CI; no write RBAC for humans or agents in
259	  prod; read roles exclude logs and exec in namespaces with claim data (mechanism: G1).
260	- **Incident lane:** label `incident`, on-call approver paged, security checks always run (S10), only
261	  slow unrelated tests skipped [design].
262	
263	**Example: Lambda timeouts at 2 a.m.** (Options §6)
264	
265	1. The incident-analysis session reads metrics and redacted logs and proposes `timeout` 30 → 90 s,
266	   memory 1024 → 2048 MB, and a larger visibility timeout on the source queue (ratio ⚠️ Options §8).
267	2. A second session (edit tools; not meant to use prod roles) edits `serverless.yml`, runs
268	   `serverless diff` on non-prod, and opens a PR labelled `incident` as the engineer.
269	3. The on-call approver reviews the diff, and can catch a missing queue change, then approves.
270	4. The deploy workflow packages, previews prod, finds no risky change, deploys with the OIDC role.
271	5. Estimate 11–46 min (⚠️ Options §6) against ≤ 30 min: measured first in rollout.
272	
273	**Audit evidence.** The PR (diff, approvers, checks); run log and preview artifact, exported because
274	retention is unverified (⚠️ G7); deploy-role CloudTrail events; all linked by commit SHA and run ID.
275	
276	**Cost / value.** One approval for routine prod changes, two for risky ones, none in non-prod.
277	Compliance gets four-eyes enforced by GitHub. Gap: on Team the prod diff is not seen before apply.

318	## Layer 5 — CI/CD hardening
319	
320	**Principle.** CI is the default production writer, so it is the main target. Short-lived,
321	least-privilege credentials per job. Every CI dependency is pinned. Agent-written code passes the same
322	checks as human code (S10).
323	
324	**On Papaya's stack**
325	
326	- **Credentials:** OIDC instead of keys and tokens in repository secrets, which any writer can read
327	  (📖 R3.4.1, R3.5.3b). `GITHUB_TOKEN` "restricted" by default, `permissions:` per job (📖 R3.5.3).
328	  "Allow GitHub Actions to create and approve pull requests" off (📖 R3.3.3). Serverless License Key in
329	  SSM, read by the deploy role (sf ≥ 4.4.19, 📖 R4.4.8). Until G1/G2 are solved, k0s and Firebase
330	  deploys may still need a stored credential: a proposed time-boxed exception to S2 = 0 (Q1).
331	- **Side paths:** Pulumi ESC, Pulumi Deployments and Serverless Dashboard providers reach AWS
332	  (📖 R4.4.9) outside the GitHub gate (⚠️ R4.4.9); not used for prod (⚠️ R4.6 #6).
333	- **Pinning:** workflow lockfile (`gh actions-lock`) or full SHA, enforced by the org policy "Require
334	  actions to be pinned to a full-length commit SHA"; the lockfile does not pin reusable workflows, so
335	  the deploy workflow lives in the same repo (📖 R3.5.5).
336	- **CODEOWNERS** on `.github/`, `CLAUDE.md`, `CLAUDE.local.md`, `.claude/`, `.claude.json`, `.mcp.json`,
337	  `.husky/`, `.gitmodules`, `.ripgreprc` (📖 R3.2.8; list ⚠️ R6.5 #5); CI validates the file, because
338	  invalid lines are skipped silently (📖 R3.2.7).
339	- **No privileged triggers with untrusted code** (`pull_request_target`, `workflow_run` + checkout,
340	  📖 R3.5.4).
341	- **Agents in CI:** `claude-code-action` with a custom GitHub App limited to Contents, Issues, Pull
342	  requests (📖 R1.7.8); Anthropic workload identity federation, not a personal OAuth token (📖 R1.7.6);
343	  `--restricted` and explicit `--tools` (D3; passing it through `claude_args` unverified, ⚠️ research
344	  6.9.4 Q5); a managed-settings file on the runner, which also guards against mods (📖 R1.5.6; for
345	  federation auth ⚠️); MCP set fixed by CI because `.mcp.json` loads without a prompt in `-p` runs
346	  (📖 R1.3.5); never `environment: production` (⚠️ R3.6 #4). Hosted runners give `sudo` (📖 R3.5.1),
347	  so with `Bash` in `--tools` the runner file is advisory (⚠️ R3.5.1, R3.6 #4).
348	- **App-opened PRs:** a required check with a pinned source app confirms at least one approval by a
349	  human who did not trigger the run; counting approvals is not enough, since the app's own approval
350	  might count (⚠️ R3.3.4, R3.7 A3; 📖 R3.2.5).
351	- **Required checks (S10):** secret scanning, dependency check, SAST (products: G4); IAM Access
352	  Analyzer `check-no-new-access` (📖 R2.8.1); Pulumi policy packs (📖 R4.2.2).
353	
354	**Audit evidence.** Workflows and lockfile in git; audit-log events such as
355	`org.update_actions_secret`, `repo.set_workflow_permission_can_approve_pr`, `repository_ruleset.update`
356	(📖 R3.3.3, R3.5.6); check results per PR; secrets inventory (S2).
357	
358	**Cost / value.** One-time migration to OIDC and pinned actions; slower action updates. Compliance

363	## Layer 6 — Data protection and prompt-injection defence
364	
365	**Principle.** PHI never reaches the coding agent (owner decision, research 1.9). Other customer
366	personal data is outside that hard boundary ("not extended", research 5.8): the agent reads metadata
367	by default and may read such data case by case under GĐ-9. Real-data reads are approved,
368	tenant-scoped, time-boxed, and need an agreement (BAA/DPA, partner contract) (GĐ-9). Everything read
369	from outside is untrusted. Non-prod is synthetic (GĐ-14).
370	
371	**On Papaya's stack**
372	
373	- **Paths to PHI** (research 1.11.4 lists 17):
374	  - AWS stores: closed by identity, through `ProdReadMetadata` from phase 1 and the SCP from phase 2
375	    (layer 1); no Aurora credentials, no prod exec, no `lambda:InvokeFunction` for agent-usable roles
376	    [design; actions ⚠️ G13];
377	  - k0s logs/exec and GCP stores (L1, L11, L13): same principle, mechanism open (G1, G3);
378	  - tickets/chat via MCP, pasted text, internal admin pages, prod AI traces, fixtures, CI logs (L5,
379	    L8–L10, L12, L14): process and hygiene only;
380	  - logs redacted at source with raw payloads in a separate log group; alerts carry IDs, not payloads [design].
381	- **Real-data request** [design]: tenant, purpose, store, window, agreement; approved by the data owner
382	  and an approver ≠ requester; JIT data-read role, 1 h. Per-tenant scoping through session tags
383	  (📖 R2.1.8) is unresolved, because tags come from user attributes (⚠️).
384	  - **PHI:** a human reads in a terminal without an agent; the agent gets a redacted summary. This
385	    narrows GĐ-9 because the agent stays outside PHI scope (research 1.9) and Team is not shown as
386	    BAA-covered (⚠️ R1.11.3.4). Enterprise + BAA only for a separate environment if needed (research 1.9).
387	  - **Non-PHI personal data:** the agent may read it within the approved request (GĐ-9).
388	- **Partner-uploaded claim documents (A7b):** never in an agent session raw; reproduce with synthetic
389	  documents, or de-identify first [design]. The document is PHI and an injection vector (research
390	  1.11.4 L6).
391	- **Injection** (these lower frequency; layers 1 and 3 limit impact): Manual by default; the auto-mode
392	  classifier missed 17 % of 52 real overeager actions (📖 R6.3.5). Broad allowed domains such as
393	  `github.com` are a documented exfiltration path (📖 R6.3.7). The incident session has no edit tools
394	  and runs outside the repo, but its Bash can still write locally and send data out through excluded
395	  commands (layer 2); what is at stake is bounded by "no standing write, no PHI read". Shared knowledge
396	  goes in `CLAUDE.md` under review; auto memory is unprotected unless `--restricted` (📖 R6.3.11, D3).
397	- **Tenants:** one tenant per data-read grant; a session that read one tenant's data does not post to
398	  shared places without review (⚠️ R6.5 #8, process). Logical separation in shared accounts is assumed
399	  (GĐ-3).
400	- **Non-prod:** no prod copies (S11). A scan of non-prod stores runs at the start of phase 1 (tool:
401	  G4); a store not yet scanned follows the L3-data rule (GĐ-14). Cost: until scanned, that store is
402	  not part of the free loop.
403	- **Local stores:** transcripts and memory hold what the agent read (research 1.11.4); set
404	  `cleanupPeriodDays` (30 in the HIPAA sample, 📖 R5.5.4; what it deletes ⚠️).
405	- **Cross-border (Vietnam example):** processing data collected in Vietnam on a platform abroad is a
406	  transfer (📖 R5.4.5); agent flows, including employee names in logs and transcripts, update the
407	  transfer impact assessment (⚠️ R5.7 #4, needs Papaya legal).
408	
409	**Audit evidence.** SCP/IAM text as the written access rule for sensitive data (📖 R5.4.3; ⚠️ R5.7 #5);
410	data-read requests and the data-read role's CloudTrail; planted-injection reports (layer 8); non-prod
411	scan results (S11).
412	
413	**Cost / value.** Debugging with redacted and synthetic data; a request for the rare real-data read.
414	Compliance gets "minimum necessary" (📖 R1.11.1.8) enforced by IAM, and a record per exception (S9).

418	## Layer 7 — Observability, audit, incident response and break-glass
419	
420	**Principle.** One tamper-evident evidence chain per prod change. One routed alert channel with a
421	named on-call, approvers included. Unapproved change is detected (drift, reconciliation). Break-glass
422	is approved before use, time-boxed and reconciled after.
423	
424	**On Papaya's stack**
425	
426	- **Audit stores:**
427	  - organization CloudTrail to a log-archive account with integrity validation (📖 R2.6.2, R2.6.4,
428	    R2.6.5); change records ≥ 6 years; raw-log retention for Papaya's compliance owner (⚠️ R5.7 #2).
429	    Data events only on PHI buckets, prod Lambda invoke and prod SQS (📖 R2.6.3), which makes the archive
430	    PHI-bearing (⚠️ research 1.11.4 L15). CloudTrail Lake is closed to new customers (📖 R2.6.6);
431	  - GitHub org audit log kept 180 days, so exported (📖 R3.5.6);
432	  - alerts on `repository_ruleset.update`, `environment.update_protection_rule`,
433	    `environment.remove_protection_rule`, `environment.delete`, `protected_branch.policy_override`
434	    (📖 R3.5.6, R3.1.4; selection ⚠️ R3.6 #1). UI changes to the branch policy may leave no event, and a
435	    deleted `production` environment comes back unprotected (⚠️ R3.1.4): a job compares live settings
436	    with an expected copy (G8);
437	  - Aurora SQL is likely invisible to CloudTrail (⚠️ R2.7.1): Database Activity Streams, alerts on
438	    lost-record events, stream treated as PHI (📖 R2.7.2; Serverless v2 ⚠️);
439	  - Claude Code OTel without prompt content (layer 2).
440	- **Change record [design]:** keyed by commit SHA or JIT request ID; links PR, approvals, run ID,
441	  preview and CloudTrail events. Monthly reconciliation: every prod write event matches a record
442	  approved before apply (S3). Actor: `onBehalfOf.userId` where present, else session name plus
443	  directory lookup (📖 R2.5.1; ⚠️ R2.5.3).
444	- **Drift [design]:** its own read role, trusted only from a `drift` environment on `main`; it can read
445	  prod secrets in state, which is noted (⚠️ R4.6 #2). Scheduled `pulumi preview --refresh
446	  --expect-no-changes` or `pulumi refresh --preview-only` (📖 R4.1.1, R4.3.1, R4.3.2); CloudFormation
447	  drift detection, explicitly set properties only (📖 R4.4.6). No auto-remediation: it is an unreviewed
448	  `pulumi up --refresh` (📖 R4.3.2). Each finding gets an actor and a ticket.
449	- **On-call:** phase 1 delivers only the named approver schedule (primary + backup, 24/7), as decided
450	  in framing round 1, including a platform approver because L3 needs one (Options §1). Alert routing and
451	  the rest of on-call follow in phase 2 (tools: G5).
452	- **Break-glass = JIT fallback** [design unless marked]:
453	
454	  | Step | Rule |
455	  |---|---|
456	  | When | The PR path cannot be used: operation not in IaC and no runbook; GitHub/Actions down; pipeline broken. The approver refuses JIT for anything expressible in IaC while the pipeline works, and records why. |
457	  | Request | Command list, scope, reason, incident link, in a channel that does not depend on GitHub. |
458	  | Approval | On-call approver ≠ requester, before the grant. |
459	  | Grant | `InfraOperator-<service>`, 1 h (📖 R2.1.4). Deleting the assignment likely stops only new sessions (⚠️ R2.4.2, R2.9 #3); ending the portal session does not end role sessions (📖 R2.4.3); an immediate stop needs the revocation SCP (📖 R2.4.4). |
460	  | Execution | The human types the commands; no agent in that terminal (D2). |
461	  | After | A job compares CloudTrail writes in the window with the list; a codify PR within a fixed deadline (as soon as GitHub is back); drift detection until it merges. |
462	  | Identity Center outage | Emergency SAML federation to roles, built and tested in advance (📖 R2.1.11; ⚠️ R2.9 #2); no user mapped until an approved activation, which is alerted. |
463	
464	  **Example request (illustrative command ⚠️):** "INC-123, `claims-doc-extract`, Actions outage. Run
465	  `aws ecs update-service --cluster <prod-cluster> --service <svc> --force-new-deployment`. Scope
466	  `InfraOperator-claims`, 1 h."
467	
468	  **Metrics** (Options §7; starting thresholds ⚠️ to calibrate): JIT used where a PR was possible
469	  (review at 1); writes outside the list (review at 1); codify PRs late (review at 1); grants per
470	  month and share of incidents needing non-IaC operations (review above about 25 %). On a breach,
471	  make the PR lane faster or add a runbook; do not widen JIT.
472	- **Roadmap:** runbooks for repeated non-IaC operations, if SSM Automation's approval step meets three
473	  conditions (Options §2; outside 02-research, G6); break-glass from an environment without the agent
474	  (D2, ⚠️).
475	
476	**Audit evidence.** Validated CloudTrail; exported GitHub audit log; change records and monthly
477	reconciliation (S3, S8 ≤ 30 min); JIT requests, reconciliations, codify PRs; drift tickets; on-call
478	schedule and approval waits (S7).
479	
480	**Cost / value.** The incident lane is slower than direct access (estimated 11–46 vs 2–20 min,
481	Options §6), and JIT needs a written command list. Compliance gets approval before apply even in
482	incidents, plus detection.

# 02 — Research: what the tools can actually do today

## English summary

- **Scope:** six topics checked against official docs, each through independent review rounds: Claude Code at org level,
  AWS identity/guardrails/audit, GitHub, Pulumi and Serverless in CI, compliance (ISO 27001, HIPAA, Vietnam as the
  regional example), and coding-agent risks (prompt injection).
- **Claude Code (Topic 1):** managed settings can lock modes, MCP, plugins and hooks, but they are client-side and not a
  security boundary. Compliance's approval rule must therefore be enforced in AWS IAM and the GitHub gate.
- **AWS (Topic 2):** on a laptop an agent using the engineer's SSO cache is indistinguishable from the engineer. The
  decisive control is no standing prod-write access for humans: changes go through CI, and human writes come only from
  approved JIT assignments. Revocation is slow by design; SCPs and an org CloudTrail are the guardrails the agent cannot edit.
- **GitHub (Topic 3):** on the Team plan, private repos have no environment approval gate, so the gate is the PR merge
  to `main`, enforced by rulesets and CODEOWNERS, with OIDC trust pinned to repo, environment and workflow.
- **Pulumi/Serverless (Topic 4):** PRs preview non-prod only, because prod preview needs state-write and secret access.
  On Team, no human sees the prod diff before apply; this gap is stated openly.
- **Compliance (Topic 5):** the "named human" rule is Papaya's chosen way to meet ISO/HIPAA controls, not a quoted
  requirement. Approval and change records are kept ≥ 6 years.
- **Agent risks (Topic 6):** design as if prompt injection succeeds. IAM and the CI gate limit impact; agent-side
  controls only reduce frequency. Balance principle (6.8): friction where damage is large, none where it is small.
- **Owner decisions (2026-11-08):** agents stay outside PHI scope; the design prepares for both MDM and no-MDM; GitHub
  Team without merge queue; customer-data scope not extended. D1: sessions start in Manual mode (a default, not a hard
  control). D2: in an incident JIT window the agent proposes and the human runs writes in a separate terminal, with a
  codify PR and drift detection. D3: `--restricted` is mandatory for write-capable and unattended sessions.

Purpose: ground every later design decision in current, official documentation, not model memory.
Written in English (it will be quoted in `docs/`); short Vietnamese notes where useful.

This applies 1.11.1 to the data the brief names. The legal text is ✅; **applying it to Papaya is

|---|---|---|

| Diagnoses (MED) | **PHI** | Same rule as medical records |
| Claim history (MED) | **PHI**, even without a diagnosis | Claims are "payment for the provision of health care" (1.11.1.1, 1.11.1.6) |
| National ID / CCCD (NID) | **PII** on its own. **Part of PHI** when it is in a member or claim record | An identifying number. Safe harbor lists "(R) any other unique identifying number" (1.11.1.7); "(G) SSN" is the US equivalent |
| Bank account (BANK) | **PII** (financial) on its own. **Part of PHI** when it is the payout account of a claim | "(J) Account numbers" is a listed identifier (1.11.1.7), and claim payout is payment for care (1.11.1.6) |
| Policy and member numbers | **Part of PHI** in claim context | "(I) Health plan beneficiary numbers" (1.11.1.7) |
| Same data, de-identified by safe harbor | **Not PHI** | 1.11.1.7. Under local law it may still be personal data (1.11.1.12, ⚠️) |
| Infrastructure metadata (resource names, metrics, config without customer values) | **Neither** | Provided it is not linked to health or claim information. The 18 identifiers are a de-identification test for health information, not a test for non-health data, so an IP address alone in an infra log is not PHI. **Deliberate safety margin:** treat IP addresses, URLs containing claim or member IDs, and object keys that contain names or ID numbers as PHI when they can be linked to a claim (1.11.1.7) |

**Practical consequence (inference ⚠️):**
- Claim records combine MED with NID and BANK, so any production store or stream that carries claim
  data should be treated as PHI-bearing as a whole: Aurora claim tables, the claim-documents S3
  bucket, and the queues and logs of claim services.
- Separating PII from PHI field by field is not a safe basis for agent access.

#### 1.11.4 Paths by which PHI can reach a DevSecOps agent's context (to handle in Phase 4)

**This is my analysis, not quoted from any document.** It lists paths to close or control, so that
"PHI never reaches the agent" holds. "Context" includes anything the agent reads: tool output, files,
fetched pages, MCP results, images. Anything in context is sent to the model provider and saved in
the local session transcript (`~/.claude*/projects/…/*.jsonl`, **local check** on this machine).
Controls are only candidates; they are designed in Phase 4.

| # | Path | How it gets into context | Why PHI is likely | Candidate controls (Phase 4) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| L1 | **Prod logs:** CloudWatch Logs from Lambda and ECS, k0s pod logs, GCP Cloud Logging | Agent runs `aws logs`, `kubectl logs`, or reads a log MCP during debug or incident | Request payloads, exception messages with record values, document-extraction output; IPs and URLs become PHI when linked to a claim | Log redaction at source; agent role reads metrics and redacted log groups only; separate log group for raw payloads with no agent access |
| L2 | **Database queries:** Aurora prod or replicas | `psql` or a DB MCP; `SELECT *` while debugging; error messages and slow-query or `pg_stat_statements` text with literals | Claim tables hold MED + NID + BANK | No DB credentials for the agent; a schema-only or masked view role; reads of real data only through the GĐ-9 exception |
| L3 | **S3:** claim documents, exports, backups | `aws s3 cp/ls`; reading a file to "check format" | Medical documents and ID scans; **object keys** may contain names or ID numbers | Deny `s3:GetObject` on PHI buckets for agent roles; consider whether `ListBucket` exposes keys |
| L4 | **Message and workflow payloads:** SQS/DLQ, SNS, Step Functions execution history | Inspecting a DLQ or execution input/output during an incident | Payloads carry claim data; Step Functions stores input/output in history | Same as L3 for `sqs:ReceiveMessage` and `states:GetExecutionHistory`; payloads carry references, not data |
| L5 | **Tickets and chat:** Linear, Slack (incl. via MCP connectors) | Agent reads an issue or thread linked from a task | Support escalations paste claim details and screenshots | Ticket hygiene rule (no PHI in tickets); scope or deny those MCP connectors; redaction bot |
| L6 | **Partner and member uploaded documents** while debugging prod AI agents (A7b in problem framing) | Engineer gives the agent a failing document to reproduce a bug | The document **is** PHI, and is also an injection vector | Reproduce with synthetic documents; a de-identification step before any document reaches the coding agent |
| L7 | **Non-prod data that is not synthetic** | Agent works freely in dev/staging (GĐ-14) | If a prod copy or dump exists in staging, PHI is there | Enforce GĐ-14: no prod → non-prod copies; scan non-prod stores |
| L8 | **Repo content:** fixtures, seed files, sample documents, notebooks committed from real data | Agent reads the repo (always) | Engineers copy "a real example" into tests | Secret/PII scanning in CI and pre-commit; review rule for fixtures |
| L9 | **CI output:** GitHub Actions logs and artifacts from jobs that touch real data | Agent reads CI logs to fix a failing job | Test or migration output that prints rows | No real data in CI; log masking |

**Where PHI goes next once it is in context (analysis).** The agent can write it to places that
last longer than the session:
- auto-memory and `CLAUDE.md` files: local, the organization's responsibility, and they can end up
  committed to git;
- commits, PR descriptions and code comments;
- Linear comments and Slack messages;
- CI logs.

GitHub, Linear, Slack and CI are third parties, outside the Anthropic BAA.

hipaa-setup says of data sent to GitHub or other services: "Your BAA with Anthropic doesn't cover
the data it sends there" (1.11.3.6). So a leak into context is not only a model-provider issue; it
can turn into a persistent copy. Phase 4 should cover these outflows as well as the inflows above.

Cross-cutting point (inference): every path above depends on **what the agent's identity is allowed
to read**. So the strongest single control for the owner decision is an agent identity with **no
data-plane read on PHI stores**: IAM, DB roles and k0s RBAC (Topics 2–3). Redaction and rules on
the Claude Code side are the second layer, consistent with 1.8 #1.

### 1.8 What this means for Papaya (inferences — to be used in the design)

These are my conclusions from the findings above, not documented facts:

1. **Policy layer exists and is real, but it is client-side.** Managed settings can lock bypass/auto
   mode, MCP, plugins and hooks (1.1, 1.2). The docs themselves say it is not a security boundary
   (1.1.7, 1.1.8), and some failure modes are silent (1.1.11). ⇒ Compliance's rule ("named human
   approves prod changes") **cannot rest on Claude Code settings**. It must be enforced where the
   agent cannot reach: AWS IAM / GitHub (Topics 2–3). Claude Code settings are a *safety and
   hygiene* layer (fewer mistakes), not the control of record.
2. **Team plan is enough for the technical policy layer, not for PHI.** Team has server-managed
   settings (1.1.5) but not the HIPAA configuration/BAA (1.6.7), ZDR (1.6.8) or the Analytics API
   (1.4.6); settings-change audit on Team is uncertain (1.1.12). ⇒ Either the design guarantees
   that **agents never see PHI/production data** (fits Topic-0 scope: non-prod is synthetic), or
   Papaya moves to Enterprise + BAA. This is a decision for Papaya (open item).
3. **Two delivery paths are needed:** server-managed for laptops; an endpoint `managed-settings.json`
   (+ `managed-mcp.json` if exclusive MCP control is wanted, + `allowedProviders`/`forceLoginOrgUUID`
   to close provider bypasses, 1.1.15) on every machine that runs an agent unattended, because
   server-managed settings do not reach CI (1.7.10) and are skipped when a provider env var is set
   (1.1.7). On **GitHub-hosted runners** there is no image to bake into: the file would be written
   by a workflow step, and the agent step must not be able to rewrite it (⚠️ depends on whether the
   agent step has sudo — check in Topic 3). Self-hosted runners or a container image are cleaner.
4. **Defaults are permissive for this context:** interactive sessions start in auto mode, where a
   classifier — not a human — approves routine actions (1.2.3); sandbox is off (1.6.1); hooks fail
   open (1.5.2); `-p` runs execute repo hooks, `env` and helpers and connect `.mcp.json` (1.7.3).
   Each needs an explicit control: org settings (`disableAutoMode`, `sandbox.enabled`), per-hook
   `onFailure: "block"` on managed hooks, and CI flags (`--setting-sources user`,
   `--settings '{"disableAllHooks": true}'`).
5. **Bash deny rules are advisory** (1.2.6), and the sandbox covers only shell commands (1.6.2).
   Keeping prod credentials away from the agent needs several layers: sandbox
   `denyRead`/`credentials` for Bash, `Read(...)` deny rules and `blockReadsOutsideWorkingDirectories`
   for file tools, env scrub (which keeps GitHub tokens, 1.6.5), or the whole process in a
   container (1.6.6). The decisive layer is still **no prod credentials on the agent's machine at
   all**, plus IAM on the AWS side.

### 2.9 What this means for Papaya (inferences — to be used in the design)

These are my conclusions from the findings above, not documented facts:

1. **On a laptop, an agent that calls the AWS CLI/SDK directly is indistinguishable from the
   engineer.**
   - **Why:** it uses the same SSO cache, and that cache reaches every role assigned to the
     engineer (2.2.1, 2.2.2). App ID is a client hint (2.2.3). Source identity is trustworthy only
     when the IdP asserts it (2.5.4).
   - **Consequence:** a separate "agent" permission set alone does not separate the two. The
     agent can still use the engineer's other roles from the same cache.
   - **The one native, server-set signal is the AWS MCP Server** (2.2.4, 2.2.5). Calls through it
     carry `aws:ViaAWSMCPService` / `aws:CalledViaAWSMCP`, usable in SCPs. They are absent (or
     false) on direct calls (2.2.5). So the signal is a control only if the agent **cannot make
     direct calls at all**.
   - **Untested design idea, not in the docs (⚠️):** an agent-only role that denies requests not
     made through MCP. AWS documents only the reverse ("deny when via MCP"). The idea helps only if
     the agent cannot reach the engineer's other credentials:
     - **With SigV4,** the local proxy reads the AWS CLI credentials as the same OS user, so this
       needs the proxy outside the agent's sandbox (1.6).
     - **With OAuth,** the MCP path itself needs no AWS CLI credentials. But the MCP client still
       holds the OAuth token, and the agent must still be kept away from the engineer's own SSO
       cache (⚠️). There is also no multi-profile.

     Without that condition, a separate role adds no control. Also to test: whether
     `aws___run_script` and `aws___get_presigned_url` downloads carry the keys. A presigned-URL
     download is made directly by the client.
   - **The decisive layer remains no standing prod-write assignment for humans** (#2). Then
     nothing running on the laptop can write to prod outside an approved, time-boxed window.
     **Inside that window,** any process on the laptop can use the grant. This is a residual risk
     to state openly.
     *(2026-11-08: the owner chose a process control for this window, see 6.6 D2.)*
2. **Changing prod: the default path is a pipeline; human write access is the exception, via JIT.**
   - **Default path:** humans hold no prod-write rights. Changes go through CI with a deploy role.
     The named-human approval happens at the CI gate (GitHub Environments, Topic 3).
   - **JIT, for the rest:** when a human needs write access (manual operations, incidents), it
     comes from a JIT assignment. AWS has no native request/approve feature (2.4.1). The options:
     - a partner product (2.4.1);
     - the TEAM sample (2.4.1b);
     - a small home-built flow on `CreateAccountAssignment` / `DeleteAccountAssignment` (2.4.2).
   - **Audit evidence:** CloudTrail records the **grant**, and its caller is the automation role.
     It does **not** record the approver. The approver's identity lives in the approval system
     (GitHub, Linear, the partner tool, TEAM). It must be linked to the grant, for example by
     request ID, and kept as audit evidence (⚠️ design).
   - **Incidents:** under GĐ-8 the incident path is the same flow with a fast approver, not a
     bypass.
   - **Outage path:** the emergency direct-federation path (2.1.11) is for an Identity Center
     outage, and needs its own approval and alerting.
3. **Revocation is slow by design.**
   - Role sessions outlive portal sessions and assignments (2.4.3). IAM's revoke button does not
     apply to permission-set roles (2.4.6).
   - Prod permission sets should use the **1-hour minimum** session duration (2.1.4).
   - Pre-deploy the `identitystore:userId` Deny SCP on the prod OU (2.4.4), and keep the
     `aws:TokenIssueTime` Deny as an org-wide kill switch (2.4.6). This is an inference (⚠️):
     scope it by `aws:PrincipalArn` so that workload roles are not hit.
   - Set the portal session length deliberately (2.1.5, 2.1.6), including the IdP session,
     which can silently extend it.
4. **SCPs are the guardrail the agent cannot edit, but only in member accounts.** Examples:
   - protect the org trail and the log archive (2.6.2);
   - deny region drift;
   - deny data-plane reads on PHI buckets and queues, except for the application roles **and**
     the approved JIT read path that GĐ-9 allows (`aws:PrincipalArn`; tenant scoping via ABAC
     session tags, 2.1.8). This supports 1.11.4 L3–L4;
   - deny destructive actions when `aws:ViaAWSMCPService` is true (2.2.5). On its own this is
     bypassed by direct CLI calls (#1), so it is a second layer, not a control.

   Constraints:
   - Keep everything out of the management account (2.3.2, 2.3.7).
   - Deny-list SCPs sit on `FullAWSAccess` (2.3.4b).
   - Limits are 10 direct attachments per target and 10,240 characters each (2.3.4).
   - RCPs add an outside-the-org boundary for S3, SQS, KMS, Secrets Manager and Logs, but not for
     Aurora, Lambda or SNS (2.3.6).
5. **Audit trail for Compliance:**
   - **Trail:** an organization trail to a separate log-archive account, with integrity validation
     and a locked-down bucket (2.6.2, 2.6.4, 2.6.5).
   - **Retention:** decide it explicitly. The default is indefinite, and MFA delete excludes
     lifecycle rules (2.6.5).
   - **Data events:** only where they matter, because of cost (2.6.3): PHI buckets, prod Lambda
     invoke, prod SQS.
   - **No CloudTrail Lake** (2.6.6).
   - **Who did it:** use `onBehalfOf.userId` in CloudTrail where present. Otherwise use the
     session name plus a lookup in the directory (⚠️, 2.5.3). The session name changes when the
     username changes, so it is not a stable key. (`identitystore:UserId` is a policy condition
     key, not a CloudTrail field.)
   - **MCP events:** do not assume AWS MCP Server events are in the trail until the selector
     question is answered (2.5.5).
   - **Aurora:** SQL is invisible to CloudTrail (2.7.1). Use Database Activity Streams or pgaudit,
     alert on the RDS events about lost records, and treat that stream as PHI (2.7.2, 2.7.3).
   - **Same gap for shell sessions:** ECS Exec and SSM shell sessions likely have the same issue
     (⚠️ not researched, 2.10).
6. **Policy changes in Pulumi PRs can be checked mechanically.** `check-no-new-access` in CI makes
   "this PR widens IAM" a visible, reviewable fact (2.8.1; ties to Topics 3–4).

### 3.6 What this means for Papaya (inferences — to be used in the design)

These are my conclusions from the findings above, not documented facts:

1. **The GitHub plan decides where the "named human approved it" gate can sit.**
   - **On Enterprise Cloud:** a `production` environment with required reviewers, prevent
     self-review, no admin bypass, and deployment branches = `main` (3.1.1–3.1.4). The approval
     is per deployment job and logged as `workflows.approve_workflow_job` (3.5.6).
   - **On Team:** environments have **no approval gate** on a private repo (3.1.2). The gate must
     be the **PR merge to `main`**, enforced by:
     - rulesets: PR required, ≥1–2 approvals, code-owner review, path-based team reviewers for
       `infra/**` and `.github/**`, dismiss stale approvals, last-push approval, an empty bypass
       list (3.2.2–3.2.4);
     - the `production` environment restricted to `main` (3.1.3).
   - **Prerequisite on both plans: the branch rule alone does not mean "only merged, approved
     code reaches prod".** Every workflow on `main` passes a "main only" rule, whatever its trigger
     (3.4.5c). So all of the following must also hold:
     - only reviewed deploy workflows may reference `production`, enforced by CODEOWNERS on
       `.github/workflows` and a CI check;
     - deploy workflows take no ref or SHA input, and deploy the commit they run on;
     - no `production` job runs on `issue_comment`, `pull_request_target` or `workflow_run`.
       A `schedule` deploy of the current `main` commit is acceptable only if it deploys that
       commit and takes no input;
     - preferably, the `sub` claim is pinned to the reusable deploy workflow (`job_workflow_ref`,
       3.4.5).

     Under these conditions, merge approval equals deploy approval on Team.
   - **Admins remain a gap.** Admins and holders of "edit repository rules" can edit rulesets,
     environments and the OIDC `sub` customisation. This is mostly logged, not prevented (3.1.4,
     3.2.2, 3.4.5). So: few admins, periodic access review, and alerts on `repository_ruleset.update`,
     `environment.update_protection_rule`, `environment.remove_protection_rule`,
     `environment.delete` and `protected_branch.policy_override`.
   - **UI changes to the branch policy may not be audited** (⚠️, 3.1.4). A deleted
     `production` environment is likely recreated without protection by the next workflow
     that references it. The deletion itself is logged (⚠️ inference, 3.1.4). So a scheduled
     job should also compare the live environment configuration with the expected one, as
     drift detection (⚠️: the REST endpoint was not researched).
   - **GĐ-5 holds only on Enterprise.** It should go back to the framing as a correction and an
     open question for Papaya.
2. **OIDC trust must pin the repository, the gate and, where possible, the workflow** (3.4.2–3.4.5c):
   - **AWS:** prod roles trust only `repo:<org>/<repo>:environment:production`, in the repo's
     `sub` format (3.4.4). Ideally a customised `sub` includes `job_workflow_ref`, because AWS
     cannot test other claims (3.4.5).
   - **GCP:** the attribute condition must restrict to the GitHub organization (required by
     Google). It can also test `job_workflow_ref`, `ref` and `event_name` directly (3.4.5b).
   - **Non-prod:** roles trust a separate environment.
   - **Secrets:** prod credentials never live in repository secrets, because anyone with write
     access can read those (3.5.3b). This removes the long-lived AWS keys from the brief (P5).
3. **Agent-authored PRs need one more rule than human PRs** (3.3.4). Opening PRs with the
   engineer's own identity keeps GitHub's built-in author rule. App-authored PRs need 2 approvals
   or a custom check whose source app is pinned. "Allow GitHub Actions to create and approve pull
   requests" stays **off** (3.3.3).
4. **CI agents and policy files:** on standard GitHub-hosted runners, an agent with shell access
   has root, so Claude Code managed settings written in the job are advisory (3.5.1, closes the
   Topic 1 question). The real limits for a CI agent are:
   - the job's `GITHUB_TOKEN` permissions (3.5.3);
   - **no** `environment: production` in any agent workflow, so it gets no prod OIDC trust
     (3.4.5c);
   - the base-branch config restore in `claude-code-action` (1.7.9).

   Self-hosted runners would allow a root-owned policy, but bring persistence risks (3.5.2).
5. **Supply chain of CI itself:**
   - Workflow lockfile or SHA pinning, enforced by org policy (3.5.5).
   - CODEOWNERS on `.github/` (3.2.8), plus CI validation of the CODEOWNERS file, because invalid
     lines fail silently (3.2.7).
   - Restricted default `GITHUB_TOKEN` (3.5.3); no `pull_request_target` with checkout (3.5.4).
6. **Audit retention gap:** the org audit log keeps 180 days (3.5.6). ISO 27001 and HIPAA evidence
   needs longer, so it must be exported periodically (JSON or CSV, within the export limits, ✅)
   or streamed (⚠️ not researched; may be Enterprise-only).

The **prod** preview runs after merge, on `main`, in the deploy workflow just before `up`. On Enterprise the environment approval could sit between the two; on Team the merge was the approval (3.6 #1). - Splitting S3 permissions so that preview can write only `locks/` is ⚠️ unverified. It probably needs `kms:Decrypt`, or Pulumi Cloud stack read, to read state that contains secrets. The drift job can then read prod secrets, which must be noted and restricted. 3. **Close the bypass paths inside the tools:** - **`serverless deploy function`** changes code **and configuration** outside CloudFormation. The change persists after the next deploy (4.4.4). In prod, deny `lambda:UpdateFunctionCode` **and** `lambda:UpdateFunctionConfiguration` to every principal except the CloudFormation `deploymentRole`. - This works only if `deploymentRole` is set. IAM cannot tell `pulumi` commands apart: the deploy role can write state anyway. So keeping state-changing commands (`state …`, `import`, `destroy`, `stack rm`) out of prod runs is enforced only by the workflow allowlist plus CODEOWNERS on `.github/` (3.2.8). Any other use needs a separately approved run. 4. **Policy as code where the agent can't switch it off.** - **Enforcement point:** the policy that counts is the one evaluated during `up` on `main` (4.2.4). - Prefer Pulumi Cloud policy groups (Essentials+) if Papaya is on Pulumi Cloud, and limit who can run `pulumi policy disable`. - Otherwise use `--policy-pack` in a CODEOWNERS-protected reusable workflow (4.2.3). - **No `remediate` level in prod** (4.2.4). - **Serverless:** the CloudFormation template from `sls package` can be checked by a CI policy tool (⚠️ tool not researched). Add IAM Access Analyzer `check-no-new-access` on changed policies (2.8.1). 5. **Drift is a compliance signal: it means an unreviewed change happened.** - **Pulumi:** scheduled `pulumi refresh --preview-only`, or `pulumi preview --refresh --expect-no-changes`. Without `--refresh`, a preview compares only against recorded state and cannot see drift (4.3.1). Or use Pulumi Cloud drift detection (Pro+), **with auto-remediation off in prod**, because it runs an unreviewed `up` (4.3.2). - **Serverless:** scheduled CloudFormation drift detection, with its coverage limits (4.4.6). It may not catch a `deploy function` code change (⚠️, 4.7). - Every drift finding maps to a CloudTrail actor (2.5) and an incident or ticket. 6. **Third-party credential paths must be closed or put under the same gate** (4.4.9). Pulumi ESC, Pulumi Deployments and Serverless Dashboard Providers each hold a path to prod. - **Default:** do not use them for prod. - **If they are used:** their AWS trust and their admin roles must be as narrow as the GitHub `production` path, and audited (Pulumi Cloud audit logs need Pro+, 4.3.5). 7. **State and secrets:** - **State buckets:** Pulumi state and Serverless state buckets are prod-sensitive stores (encrypted secrets, resource outputs). Restrict them to the deploy roles (4.3.3, 4.4.1). - **Pulumi secrets:** use `awskms` as the secrets provider on a DIY backend (4.3.4). - **Serverless secrets:** resolve them at runtime, not baked into templates (⚠️ 4.4.7). - **Serverless License Key:** keep it in SSM per account, read by the deploy role (≥ 4.4.19). This avoids a long-lived GitHub secret (4.4.8, 3.5.3b).

HIPAA and Vietnam citations are ✅ text. **The "evidence" column is my inference (⚠️)**: it lists what the design must produce so that an auditor can test the control. | Area | ISO 27001:2022 Annex A (⚠️) | HIPAA Security Rule | Vietnam (example) | Evidence the design must produce | |---|---|---|---|---| | Production change | 8.32, 8.31, 8.25, 8.9, 5.3, 8.4 | 164.308(a)(1)(ii)(B) risk management; 164.312(c) integrity; 164.316(b) records for 6 years | No change-control article. Suppliers include Anthropic, GitHub, AWS, Google (GCP and Firebase), Pulumi, Serverless Inc., Linear and Slack (both may hold PHI, 1.11.4), and each approved MCP server or plugin publisher | ### 5.7 What this means for Papaya (inferences — to be used in the design) 1. **The "named human" rule is policy, not a quoted requirement (⚠️).** Neither the HIPAA text (5.2.10) nor, as far as I recall, ISO Annex A (5.1.8) literally requires "a named human approves every prod change". Both require unique identity, audit controls, integrity and records. So the design should present the Compliance rule as Papaya's chosen way to meet 8.32 / 5.3 and 164.312(a)(2)(i) / (b) / (c). The record chain in 5.6 is what proves it to an auditor. 2. **Retention value: at least 6 years for approval and change records.** 164.316(b)(2)(i) requires 6-year retention of required documentation (5.2.9). Whether raw audit logs themselves must be kept 6 years is interpretation (⚠️). Topic 2 already plans an organization trail to a log-archive account with an explicit retention decision (2.9); this sets the value for approval and change records. **New item:** the GitHub org audit log keeps 180 days (3.5.6), so the GitHub side needs its own export. 3. **Emergency access (⚠️ mapping).** HIPAA requires a documented procedure for obtaining ePHI during an emergency (5.2.6). It does not speak about production changes. A break-glass path to prod is one common way to support it, and the agreed "incident approvals within 15 min, 24/7" is Papaya's policy for emergency changes. Either way, the emergency path must leave the same evidence as the normal one. 4. **Cross-border transfer in the Vietnam example (⚠️ inference).** A Claude session is a platform outside Vietnam (5.4.5). If it processed personal data collected in Vietnam, that would be a cross-border transfer. If Papaya already moves Vietnamese personal data to foreign cloud, it already holds (or owes) a transfer impact assessment, and agent data flows would be an **update** to it (Art. 20(3), Art. 22), not a new duty. Two cautions: - "Infrastructure metadata" is not automatically free of personal data: CloudTrail events, git history and session transcripts contain **employee** names and emails. Two exemptions concern employee data: Law Art. 20(6)(b) (storing own employees' data on cloud) and Decree Art. 17(3)(d) (cross-border HR management). Whether sending employee identities in logs to a model provider falls under either is ⚠️. - Extending the owner's PHI decision (1.9) from PHI to **all customer personal data** (including basic data such as ID numbers, 5.4.3) is a scope change. It is a question for the owner, not a settled decision (5.8). **Owner decided 2026-11-08: not extended (5.8).** 5. **Sensitive data needs written access rules** (Decree Art. 4(2), 5.4.3). The Topic 2 design of no data-plane access for agent identities (2.9; PHI paths in 1.11.4) is the matching control, and its SCP/IAM text is the written rule. 6. **The NPRM shows where the requirements are heading** (5.3.2): MFA on all relevant ePHI systems and for privilege changes, real-time monitoring and recording of activity, yearly vendor verification and an asset inventory. MFA through Identity Center and a supplier register are cheap. Real-time monitoring of **all** activity is not: CloudTrail data events cover only the RDS Data API, not SQL sent over database connections (⚠️ inference, 2.7.1). The design should label these as forward-looking, not as current requirements. 7. **Supplier register entries are concrete** (5.5.1–5.5.3): Anthropic and GitHub certificates are self-service for org owners or via the Trust Portal. The GCP BAA covers Agent Platform generative AI but **not Firebase**, so Firebase Hosting must stay PHI-free (consistent with a static front end, ⚠️ not verified for Papaya). 8. **Team-plan limits remain visible.** Tenant Restrictions (5.5.6) is available to Enterprise plans and Console organizations, so a Team org cannot use it to block claude.ai sign-ins to other organizations (⚠️ inference). Stopping use of personal accounts on corporate code then depends on network and device controls (MDM is unknown, 1.9). `settings-hipaa.json` (5.5.4) is still a good **template** for Team managed settings, key by key, subject to Topic 1's plan notes. The README says it applies "whether or not the HIPAA configuration is in effect", and that the same keys must also go into server-managed settings if the org uses them (5.5.4). 9. **Risk-register input from the README** (5.5.5, 5.5.5b): the laptops' managed file does not reach the Claude Code GitHub Action, so CI needs its own runner-side file (1.7.10 b), which can be tampered with on hosted runners (3.5.1). Injected instructions are limited only by the sandbox network allowlist, and in auto mode a classifier, not a person, approves actions.
